}}'''''Commiphora myrrha''''', called '''myrrh''',<ref name="grin"/> '''Somali myrrh''',<ref name="grin"/> '''herabol myrrh''',<ref name="grin"/> '''common myrrh''',<ref name="Kynes2013">{{cite book |vauthors=Kynes S |title=Mixing Essential Oils for Magic: Aromatic Alchemy for Personal Blends |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=oeINAQAAQBAJ&pg=PA191 |date=8 November 2013 |publisher=Llewellyn Worldwide |isbn=978-0-7387-3715-7 |pages=191–}}</ref> is a tree in the family [[Burseraceae]]. It is one of the primary trees used in the production of [[myrrh]], a resin made from dried tree [[sap]]. The Commiphora myrrha tree is indigenous to [[Somalia]], in the Somali regions of [[Ethiopia]] and [[Kenya]], [[Djibouti]], [[Eritrea]] and parts of the [[Arabian Peninsula]] ([[Yemen]] and  [[Oman]]).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.cactus-art.biz/schede/COMMIPHORA/Commiphora_myrrha/Commiphora_myrrha/Commiphora_myrrha.htm |title=''Commiphora myrrha'' |work=Cactus art: The world of cacti & succulents |access-date=2009-01-15}}</ref> 

Myrrh is a fragrant gum resin that is similar to frankincense. The tree species that produces myrrh (Commiphora myrrha) thrives well in the arid and semi-arid regions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Schmiedebergs |first1=Naunyn |title=Commiphora myrrh: a phytochemical and pharmacological update |journal=Naunyn-Schmiedeberg's Archives of Pharmacology |date=2023 |volume=396 |issue=3 |pages=405–420 |publisher=National Library of Medicine |doi=10.1007/s00210-022-02325-0 |pmid=36399185 |pmc=9672555 }}</ref> [[Somalia]] is the largest producer of both myrrh and [[frankincense]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Riegler |first1=Dan |title=A complete guide to Frankincense resins |url=https://apothecarysgarden.com/blogs/blog/a-guide-to-the-different-types-of-frankincense#:~:text=of%20Frankincense%20resin.-,Frankincense%20Carterii%2DSomalia,than%20Frankincense%20Sacra%20and%20Dalzielii. |website=Apothecary's Garden |date=4 December 2023 |access-date=4 December 2023}}</ref> 

Myrrh has been used historically for over 3,000 years.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Geist |first1=Linda |title=Frankincense and myrrh: Ancient scents of the season |url=https://extension.missouri.edu/news/frankincense-and-myrrh-ancient-scents-of-the-season |website=MU Extension |publisher=University of Missouri |access-date=15 December 2022}}</ref> Evidence of its use may be found as far back as the early days of [[ancient Egypt]]. It was employed there for embalming in a manner akin to that of [[frankincense]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Geist |first1=Linda |title=Frankincense and myrrh: Ancient scents of the season |url=https://extension.missouri.edu/news/frankincense-and-myrrh-ancient-scents-of-the-season |website=MU Extension |publisher=University of Missouri |access-date=15 December 2022}}</ref> However, the raw material has also been used as incense for a very long time. Myrrh was and is still used for ceremonial incense and anointing in a number of nations, including [[Somalia]], [[Ethiopia]], [[Sudan]], and [[Yemen]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Unlocking the Mystique of Myrrh and Its Role in Perfumery |url=https://www.alphaaromatics.com/blog/myrrh-in-perfumery/#:~:text=It%20is%20believed%20to%20have,tree%20are%20her%20eternal%20tears. |website=Alpha Aromatics | date=4 October 2023 |access-date=4 October 2023}}</ref> 

==Description==
[[File:Commiphora myrrha.jpg|left|thumb|259x259px|Spiny branches of C. myrrha]]
''Commiphora myrrha'' is very spiny and it grows to a height of about {{cvt|5|m|ft}}.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=''Commiphora myrrha'' |url=https://www.cactus-art.biz/schede/COMMIPHORA/Commiphora_myrrha/Commiphora_myrrha/Commiphora_myrrha.htm |access-date=2022-12-05 |website=www.cactus-art.biz}}</ref> Its short, hairless, thick, and flaky trunk has two layers of bark. The upper layer is silvery, whitish, reddish, or bluish-grey and has a papery-texture. Underneath it, the bark is green and performs photosynthesis.

Due to this species' high variability, ''Commiphora myrrha'' can be difficult to distinguish from other species within the ''Commiphora'' genus.<ref name=":42">{{Cite web |title=Myrrh - American Botanical Council |url=https://www.herbalgram.org/resources/herbalgram/issues/93/table-of-contents/herbalgram-93-herb-profile-myrrh/ |access-date=2022-12-05 |website=www.herbalgram.org}}</ref> The leaves of ''Commiphora myrrha'' are a greyish-green colour with a papery texture.<ref name=":2" /> The plant's leaves may come in an oblong or oval shape and are between 6-44mm long, and 3-20mm wide.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":32">{{Cite web |title=''Commiphora myrrha'' Myrrh, Myrrh Gum PFAF Plant Database |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Commiphora+myrrha |access-date=2022-12-05 |website=pfaf.org}}</ref> Each leaf alternates and consists of three leaflets in a pinnately compound arrangement.<ref name=":2" />

The plant's yellow-red flowers are dioecious and are arranged in a panicle inflorescence.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":32" /> The flowers of the common myrrh are very tiny and are oval shaped. The male flowers are only 3-4mm long and flower early. Its smooth, brown fruit is about the same size as the flowers, and is shaped like an egg.

=== Resin ===
From the stem of ''Commiphora myrrha'', its oleoresin oozes from incisions in the bark and dries into small clumps of sap.<ref name=":22">{{Cite web |title=Commiphora myrrha |url=https://www.cactus-art.biz/schede/COMMIPHORA/Commiphora_myrrha/Commiphora_myrrha/Commiphora_myrrha.htm |access-date=2022-12-05 |website=www.cactus-art.biz}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Myrrh - American Botanical Council |url=https://www.herbalgram.org/resources/herbalgram/issues/93/table-of-contents/herbalgram-93-herb-profile-myrrh/ |access-date=2022-12-05 |website=www.herbalgram.org}}</ref> The resin's fragrance and its medicinal properties come from the various classes of [[terpenoid]]s it contains.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |display-authors=6 |vauthors=Batiha GE, Wasef L, Teibo JO, Shaheen HM, Zakariya AM, Akinfe OA, Teibo TK, Al-Kuraishy HM, Al-Garbee AI, Alexiou A, Papadakis M |date=November 2022 |title=Commiphora myrrh: a phytochemical and pharmacological update |journal=Naunyn-Schmiedeberg's Archives of Pharmacology |volume=396 |issue=3 |pages=405–420 |doi=10.1007/s00210-022-02325-0 |pmc=9672555 |pmid=36399185}}</ref> Additionally, the common myrrh tastes sour, bitter, and aromatic.

=== Distribution and habitat ===
Native to eastern and northeastern Africa and the Arabian peninsula, this plant grows on slopes and valleys in desert regions with open ''Vachellia''.<ref name=":42" /><ref name=":32" /><ref name=":22" /> It grows at an elevation of approximately {{cvt|250|to|1300|m|ft}} with a yearly mean rainfall of about {{cvt|23|to|30|cm|in}}. It does best in thin soil, primarily in areas with limestone.<ref name="worldagro">{{cite web |title=Commiphora myrrha Species Information |url=http://www.worldagroforestrycentre.org/sea/products/afdbases/af/asp/SpeciesInfo.asp?SpID=17990 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110930043102/http://www.worldagroforestrycentre.org/sea/products/afdbases/af/asp/SpeciesInfo.asp?SpID=17990 |archive-date=2011-09-30 |access-date=2009-01-15 |publisher=World of Forestry Centre}}</ref>[[File:Commiphora-myrrha-resin-myrrh.jpg|thumb|right|Myrrh, the hardened resin extracted from ''Commiphora myrrha'']]

=== History ===
Myrrh extracted from ''Commiphora myrrha'' was a precious commodity in the ancient world, as it was used to create perfumes and incense.<ref name=":22" /> Myrrh was traditionally used in the ancient world as an insect repellent, incense for religious rituals and in embalming the dead.<ref name=":32" /><ref name=":22" /> Physicians also took advantage of its medicinal properties, treating it for several ailments, including wounds, diseases such as [[leprosy]] and [[syphilis]], and to help with digestion and menstruation.

== Medicinal properties ==
It is anti-bacterial, anti-fungal, anti-pest and can be used for fumigation or oral use.<ref name=":0" /> It has been used as an astringent, antiseptic, anti-parasitic, anti-viral anti-tussive, [[emmenagogue]], and anti-spasmodic agent. It was commonly included in mixtures used to treat worms, wounds, and sepsis. It is also a potent treatment for [[gingivitis]], [[canker sores]], [[sore throat]], [[Boil (infection)|boil]]s, [[arthritis]], and [[acne]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=El Ashry |first1=E. S. H. |last2=Rashed |first2=N. |last3=Salama |first3=O. M. |last4=Saleh |first4=A. |date=2003-03-01 |title=Components, therapeutic value and uses of myrrh |url=https://www.ingentaconnect.com/content/govi/pharmaz/2003/00000058/00000003/art00001#expand/collapse |journal=Die Pharmazie |volume=58 |issue=3 |pages=163–168|pmid=12685809 }}</ref> Due to its medicinal properties, it is imagined as a potential preventative and therapeutic agent for several diseases, including COVID-19.<ref name=":0" />

== Modern uses ==
Resin from ''Commiphora myrrha'' continues to be an important source of myrrh, which is a key ingredient that adds flavour to meat products, desserts, soft drinks, gum, and sweets.<ref name=":42" /> Moreover, its use as a fragrance in incense has extended to other cosmetic products, such as mouthwash,<ref name=":32" /> soaps, and perfumes.
